title: Streaming session lifecycle and context handoffs for Go SDK
creator: Ethan Brooks
description: Problem: Current Go SDK streaming APIs have awkward cancellation semantics that lead to goroutine leaks, inconsistent deadline propagation across layers, and unclear behavior when retries or resumable sessions are involved. This ticket scopes a focused implementation and API surface changes to make session lifecycle explicit, provide ergonomic helpers for context/timeouts, and guarantee deterministic terminal state semantics (retryable vs non-retryable).\n\nGoal: Implement a StreamSession abstraction and small set of helpers (WithStreamTimeout, StreamContextWrap) to centralize cancellation & deadline handoffs, add explicit CloseGracefully/Abort semantics, and ensure SDK integration tests cover cancellation races and timeout ordering. Ensure backwards compatibility for the most common patterns while giving advanced users explicit control over session handoff and retryability.
acceptance_criteria: A StreamSession type exists in the Go SDK that wraps the underlying grpc/http stream and context plus a session ID and resume token metadata
Helpers: WithStreamTimeout(ctx, dur) and StreamContextWrap(parentCtx) implemented and documented with examples

CloseGracefully(timeout) will signal graceful drain and wait for in-flight aggregation up to timeout, then send final FIN message. Abort() will immediately cancel underlying transport and mark session terminal non-retryable
Deadlines propagate in a well-defined order: user-provided context deadline overrides WithStreamTimeout but CloseGracefully enforces a minimum grace period if configured
No goroutine leaks detected in unit and integration tests simulating mid-stream cancellation, fast client cancel, and server-initiated termination
Metrics emitted: stream.sessions_started, stream.sessions_closed_gracefully, stream.sessions_aborted, stream.cancellation_races_detected
Documentation updated with code examples and migration notes; two sample apps showing graceful shutdown and interrupt handling
proposed_design: Introduce StreamSession struct: {ID string, ctx context.Context, cancel func(), done chan struct{}, resumeToken string, state enum{Open, Draining, Closed, Aborted}}
Expose constructor: NewStreamSession(parent context.Context, opts ...StreamOption) which returns (*StreamSession, error)
StreamOption flags: WithMinDrain time.Duration, EnableResume bool, InstrumentationKey string
API ergonomics: keep existing Reader-like streaming APIs but add session methods: s.CloseGracefully(ctx, timeout), s.Abort(), s.Resume(token) and a s.Done() channel for waiters

Retry model: SDK will only auto-retry if session state is Closed and server returned an idempotent resume token. Abort() marks non-retryable terminal state and will not be retried by the client library

Context/Deadline ordering: explicit helpers WithStreamTimeout(ctx,d) set a soft deadline for per-response read loops; user context cancellation always takes precedence for immediate shutdown. CloseGracefully may override soft deadlines to allow minimal drain (configurable via WithMinDrain).

Transport contract: introduce a small FIN frame on the wire to indicate graceful completion so server can flush aggregates. If FIN is not acked within timeout, client will escalate to Abort() and cancel transport.
Backwards compatibility: default StreamOption preserves current behavior (EnableResume=false, MinDrain=200ms). Migration guide describes when to enable resume and implications for server-side state.
implementation_notes: Files to change: sdk/go/stream/session.go (new), sdk/go/stream/transport.go (handle FIN/ACK), sdk/go/stream/examples/graceful_shutdown_example.go
Add a thin adapter in sdk/go/compat/legacy_stream.go to map existing streaming client calls into StreamSession for drop-in use
Testing harness: extend test/server-sim to emit delayed FIN acks and inject mid-stream errors; add race-detector unit tests (go test -race)
Performance: keep allocations minimal (reuse buffers, single goroutine for read loop), measure p50/p95 add'l latency from StreamSession bookkeeping (target <0.2ms overhead per-connection)
Telemetry: emit Open/Drain/Close/Abort events with session ID and latency to telemetry pipeline (opentelemetry compatible)
Docs: RFC stored at https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Go+SDK+Stream+Session+Lifecycle (link added to related_links)

Edge case: when parent context carries a deadline earlier than CloseGracefully timeout, CloseGracefully should prefer a short-circuit behavior and return an explicit ErrDeadlineConflict so callers can decide to extend deadlines or Abort.
test_plan: Unit tests: session lifecycle transitions (Open->Draining->Closed/Aborted) under direct cancel, graceful close, and transport failure
Race tests: run go test -race on new session code paths with combinatorial concurrency (Read loop + CloseGracefully + Abort + Cancel) to catch races
Integration: simulated server that delays FIN ACKs; verify client escalates to Abort after timeout and partial outputs are handled correctly
Compatibility tests: run existing SDK tests against the compat adapter to ensure no regressions
Load test: 5k parallel stream sessions for 5m with random cancels to measure goroutine profiles and CPU/alloc overhead
Observability: dashboard panel validating session lifecycle metrics and a nightly job that fails the PR pipeline if cancellation_race rate increases > 1%
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: subtle races between user cancel() and internal CloseGracefully leading to double-close. Mitigation: single compare-and-swap on session.state transitions and idempotent Abort/Close calls.

Risk: new FIN/ACK semantics require runtime server changes. Mitigation: feature-flag FIN frames and default to legacy close semantics until runtime rollout completes; compatibility adapter added on server to accept FIN frames.

Risk: enabling resume semantics may result in duplicate side-effects for non-idempotent streams. Mitigation: require server-side resume token and explicitly document that resume must only be enabled when requests are idempotent or the application tolerates duplicates.

Risk: increased CPU/alloc from bookkeeping. Mitigation: benchmark changes and micro-optimizations (sync.Pool reuse, single read goroutine), and fallback to legacy path under high-throughput configurations.
related_links: Incident: https://redwood.ai/incident/2024-11-midstream-cancel (postmortem - lessons learned about goroutine leaks)
